section.title: The Sabbath Year and the Jubilee
section.sectionRationale: This chapter extends the Sabbath principle from days to years, establishing the sabbatical year of rest for the land and, climactically, the fiftieth year Jubilee, when debts are released, land returns to its original families, and enslaved Israelites go free, grounded in the truth that the land belongs to the LORD.
section.thesis: God builds rest and restoration into the very structure of time, sabbatical years releasing the land and the Jubilee year releasing people and property, because the land is His and Israel are His redeemed servants, never permanently bound to poverty or slavery.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the Sabbath year of rest for the land; the fiftieth year Jubilee, proclaiming liberty and the return of property; laws of fair dealing in land sales and redemption tied to the Jubilee; and laws protecting the poor and enslaved countryman, since Israel are servants of the LORD alone.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses on Mount Sinai,
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them: When you enter the land that I am giving you, the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.
For six years you may sow your field and prune your vineyard and gather its crops.
But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of complete rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You are not to sow your field or prune your vineyard.
You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines. The land must have a year of complete rest.
Whatever the land yields during the Sabbath year shall be food for you, for yourself, your manservant and maidservant, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you,
and for your livestock and the wild animals in your land. All its growth may serve as food.

media.alt: A ram's horn sounding across a landscape
media.caption: The horn sounds throughout the land, proclaiming liberty in the Year of Jubilee.

verses.text: And you shall count off seven Sabbaths of years, seven times seven years, so that the seven Sabbaths of years amount to forty-nine years.
Then you are to sound the horn far and wide on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. You shall sound it throughout your land.

So you are to consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim {{deror|liberty}} in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your {{yovel|Jubilee}}, when each of you is to return to his property and to his clan.
The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.
For it is a Jubilee; it shall be holy to you. You may eat only the crops taken directly from the field.
In this Year of Jubilee, each of you shall return to his own property.

units.label: Fair dealing between neighbors
units.note: priced according to years until Jubilee

verses.text: If you make a sale to your neighbor or a purchase from him, you must not take advantage of each other.
You are to buy from your neighbor according to the number of years since the last Jubilee; he is to sell to you according to the number of harvest years remaining.
You shall increase the price in proportion to a greater number of years, or decrease it in proportion to a lesser number of years; for he is selling you a given number of harvests.
Do not take advantage of each other, but fear your God; for I am the LORD your God.
You are to keep My statutes and carefully observe My judgments, so that you may dwell securely in the land.
Then the land will yield its fruit, so that you can eat your fill and dwell in safety in the land.
Now you may wonder, ‘What will we eat in the seventh year if we do not sow or gather our produce?’
But I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year, so that the land will yield a crop sufficient for three years.
While you are sowing in the eighth year, you will be eating from the previous harvest, until the ninth year’s harvest comes in.

units.label: The land is Mine, and redemption
units.note: a kinsman may buy it back

verses.text: The {{aretz|land}} must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.
Thus for every piece of property you possess, you must provide for the {{geullah|redemption}} of the land.
If your brother becomes impoverished and sells some of his property, his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.
Or if a man has no one to redeem it for him, but he prospers and acquires enough to redeem his land,
he shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property.

But if he cannot obtain enough to repay him, what he sold will remain in possession of the buyer until the Year of Jubilee. In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.

units.label: Houses in the city, and Levite cities

verses.text: If a man sells a house in a walled city, he retains his right of redemption until a full year after its sale; during that year it may be redeemed.
If it is not redeemed by the end of a full year, then the house in the walled city is permanently transferred to its buyer and his descendants. It is not to be released in the Jubilee.
But houses in villages with no walls around them are to be considered as open fields. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the Jubilee.
As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites always have the right to redeem their houses in the cities they possess.

So whatever belongs to the Levites may be redeemed, a house sold in a city they possess, and must be released in the Jubilee, because the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the Israelites.
But the open pastureland around their cities may not be sold, for this is their permanent possession.
Now if your countryman becomes destitute and cannot support himself among you, then you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.
Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you.
You must not lend him your silver at interest or sell him your food for profit.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan and to be your God.

units.label: An Israelite who sells himself
units.note: a hired worker, not a slave

verses.text: If a countryman among you becomes destitute and sells himself to you, then you must not force him into slave labor.
Let him stay with you as a hired worker or temporary resident; he is to work for you until the Year of Jubilee.
Then he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.
Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves.
You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.
Your menservants and maidservants shall come from the nations around you, from whom you may purchase them.
You may also purchase them from the foreigners residing among you or their clans living among you who are born in your land. These may become your property.
You may leave them to your sons after you to inherit as property; you can make them slaves for life. But as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.

units.label: Redemption from a foreign master
units.note: released, at the latest, in the Jubilee

verses.text: If a foreigner residing among you prospers, but your countryman dwelling near him becomes destitute and sells himself to the foreigner or to a member of his clan,
he retains the right of redemption after he has sold himself. One of his brothers may redeem him:
either his uncle or cousin or any close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he prospers, he may redeem himself.

He and his purchaser will then count the time from the year he sold himself up to the Year of Jubilee. The price of his sale will be determined by the number of years, based on the daily wages of a hired hand.
If many years remain, he must pay for his redemption in proportion to his purchase price.
If only a few years remain until the Year of Jubilee, he is to calculate and pay his redemption according to his remaining years.
He shall be treated like a man hired from year to year, but a foreign owner must not rule over him harshly in your sight.
Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.
For the Israelites are My servants. They are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.

deror.gloss: Liberty, release, or free flow. This exact word is echoed by Isaiah, proclaim liberty to the captives, Isaiah 61:1, which Jesus reads aloud in Luke 4 and declares fulfilled in Himself, tying the Jubilee directly to His own announced mission.

yovel.gloss: Jubilee, likely from the ram's horn, yovel, sounded to announce it. Every fiftieth year, land returned to its original family and enslaved Israelites went free, a structural, repeated reset against permanent poverty and bondage.

geullah.gloss: Redemption, the act of a near relative buying back land or a person from poverty or servitude. This kinsman redeemer role, later embodied by Boaz for Ruth and Naomi, becomes a central biblical picture fulfilled in Christ's redemption of His people.

aretz.gloss: Land, earth, or territory. Verse 23's declaration, the land is Mine, relativizes every human claim to permanent ownership, grounding Israel's entire economic system in the reality that they are tenants and stewards, not ultimate possessors, of what God gives.

basic.context: This chapter establishes two rhythms of rest: every seventh year the land itself rests, and every forty-ninth year's Day of Atonement, a Jubilee is proclaimed in which debts are released, land returns to its original family, and enslaved Israelites go free.
basic.hermeneutics: This is specific old covenant economic law tied to Israel's unique tribal land inheritance in Canaan; it is not a directly transferable blueprint for modern economic policy. Its enduring vision, that poverty and bondage are not to be permanent, finds its complete fulfillment when Jesus announces true liberty in Luke 4.
basic.originalLanguages: Deror, liberty, is the very word Isaiah later uses of a coming proclamation of release, which Jesus reads aloud and declares fulfilled in Himself. Yovel, Jubilee, likely from the ram's horn sounded to announce it, names this fiftieth year reset. Ge'ullah, redemption, describes a kinsman buying back what poverty had cost his relative, grounded in the declaration that the aretz, land, ultimately belongs to God alone.
basic.typology: The Jubilee's proclamation of liberty is fulfilled when Jesus reads Isaiah's Jubilee language in the Nazareth synagogue and declares it fulfilled that very day in Himself, Luke 4:18-21. The kinsman redeemer who buys back a relative's lost land or freedom anticipates Christ, who became one of us to redeem us from slavery to sin.
basic.christ: Luke 4:18-21 records Jesus reading Isaiah's words, the Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, to proclaim liberty to the captives, in the Nazareth synagogue, then declaring, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, directly claiming the Jubilee's ancient promise as His own present mission.
basic.god: God insists the land is His, relativizing every human claim to permanent wealth or power; He builds structural, repeated points of release into Israel's economic life so that poverty, debt, and slavery are never treated as permanent, reflecting His own character as Redeemer.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:18-21 records Jesus announcing Jubilee fulfillment in Himself. Isaiah 61:1-2 supplies the source text He reads. Galatians 4:4-5 says God sent His Son to redeem those under the law. Ruth 4 shows Boaz acting as kinsman redeemer, foreshadowing this pattern.
basic.oneStory: God built repeated, structural release into Israel's calendar so that no family's poverty or bondage would ever be treated as final. That pattern of release finds its true and lasting fulfillment when Christ announces, and accomplishes, true liberty for captives to sin, redeeming His people not for fifty years but forever.

context.literary:
Verse 1 places this speech 'on Mount Sinai,' and the same location returns in Leviticus 26:46 and 27:34. The notice gathers chapters 25 to 27 together as the closing words of the Sinai legislation and reminds the reader that economic law is covenant law, given in the same place as the Ten Commandments.

The chapter is built on sevens. The land rests in the seventh year, verses 2 to 7; seven sabbaths of years, forty-nine years, lead to the fiftieth, verses 8 to 12. The sabbath principle that governs Israel's week in Leviticus 23:3 is extended to the calendar of a lifetime.

The second half, verses 25 to 55, descends in stages, each introduced by the same phrase about a brother who 'becomes impoverished' or 'destitute,' verses 25, 35, 39 and 47. First he sells part of his land, verse 25. Next he cannot support himself and needs a loan, verse 35. Then he sells his labour to a fellow Israelite, verse 39. Finally, the lowest point, he sells himself to a foreigner, verse 47. At each rung the law lays down a remedy: redemption by kin, a loan without interest, treatment as a hired worker, redemption from the foreign master, and at the last, the Jubilee that releases what nothing else has.

Refrains bind the chapter together. 'Fear your God' comes in verses 17, 36 and 43, always where a stronger party is tempted to exploit a weaker one. 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' comes in verses 38, 42 and 55, and the chapter ends on it. Every regulation is anchored in the exodus: the God who freed Israel will not let Israelites re-enslave one another. The central sentence, 'the land ... is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me,' verse 23, is the hinge between the calendar of the first half and the redemption law of the second.
context.historical:
Israel's land was to be divided 'by lot' among tribes, clans and families, Numbers 26:55, and the Jubilee protected that original distribution. In an agrarian society, land was not simply wealth; it was the family's means of life and its place in the covenant people. Once a family lost its fields, debt tended to deepen into servitude. Naboth's refusal to sell to Ahab, 'The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers,' 1 Kings 21:3, shows how seriously this was held, and Isaiah's woe on those who 'add house to house and join field to field,' Isaiah 5:8, shows how badly it was later violated.

The sale envisaged in verses 14 to 16 was really a lease of harvests. The price was set by the number of crop years remaining until the Jubilee, because the buyer was purchasing produce, not the land itself. Walled city houses, verses 29 and 30, could pass permanently after one year, since they were not agricultural inheritance; village houses counted with the fields. The Levites, who had no tribal territory, held their cities and pasturelands, Numbers 35:2, and those were protected even more strongly, verses 32 to 34.

Rulers elsewhere in the ancient Near East sometimes issued edicts cancelling debts and freeing debt slaves, usually at the start of a reign, as royal favours. Israel's release was different in kind: it was fixed in the calendar by God's law and did not depend on a king's generosity.

The Jubilee horn sounded 'on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement,' verse 9. The year of release began on the day the sanctuary and people were cleansed. Whether the Jubilee was ever fully kept is uncertain. The seventh year release was neglected, as Jeremiah 34:14 laments and 2 Chronicles 36:21 implies, and Nehemiah's community had to pledge afresh to 'let the fields lie fallow' and 'cancel every debt,' Nehemiah 10:31.
context.canonical:
The Sabbath year here builds on Exodus 23:10-11, where the fallow year feeds 'the poor among your people' and 'the wild animals,' and Deuteronomy 15 adds the cancellation of debts and the release of Hebrew servants every seventh year. Leviticus 25 adds the fiftieth year and the return of land.

The prophets take up the chapter's vocabulary. Jeremiah 34:8-17 records Zedekiah's covenant 'to proclaim liberty' to slaves and the people's betrayal of it, to which God answers, 'I proclaim freedom for you ... to fall by sword.' Ezekiel's vision of the restored land assumes 'the year of freedom,' Ezekiel 46:17. Isaiah 61:1-2 turns the Jubilee into the mission of the Spirit-anointed servant: 'to proclaim liberty to the captives ... to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor.' Isaiah 49:8 speaks of the servant appointed 'to restore the land, to apportion its desolate inheritances.'

In Luke 4:18-21 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and inserts a line from Isaiah 58:6, 'to release the oppressed,' so that release is sounded twice. The language of redemption runs on through Ruth 4 and Jeremiah 32, where Jeremiah buys his cousin's field 'for you have the right of redemption,' Jeremiah 32:7, as a pledge that Israel will return to its land.

The New Testament gathers the chapter's themes. Believers are 'foreigners and exiles,' 1 Peter 2:11, echoing verse 23. Christ shares our flesh 'to free those who all their lives were held in slavery,' Hebrews 2:15. The church in Acts, where 'there were no needy ones among them,' Acts 4:34, recalls the hope of Deuteronomy 15:4. And Paul looks to the day creation 'will be set free from its bondage to decay,' Romans 8:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to understand that their land, labour and liberty were gifts held in trust from the LORD, not possessions to be traded without limit. Verse 23 states the principle: the land is God's, and Israel lives on it as His guests. Everything else follows. A field can be leased, but not sold forever. A brother can be hired, but not owned. A loan can be made, but not used to profit from his need.

He also meant to shape the heart as well as the market. The instruction to 'fear your God,' repeated at every point where exploitation is possible, verses 17, 36 and 43, calls Israel to see the LORD standing behind every bargain between neighbours. The anticipated objection of verse 20, 'What will we eat in the seventh year?' is answered by promise: 'I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year,' verse 21. Keeping the Sabbath year was an act of trust, like gathering double manna on the sixth day, Exodus 16:29.

Finally, he meant Israel to remember who they were. They were servants whom God had brought out of Egypt, verse 42, and a redeemed people must not become a nation of slave masters. The same story of rescue that gave them their identity was to govern how they treated the poor among them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescription for Israel in the land: commands about sowing, pricing, redemption, interest and servitude. It presupposes a tribal land allotment that no modern nation or church possesses, and it speaks within an ancient economy that included debt service and foreign slavery, verses 44 to 46, which it regulates rather than creates.

What carries forward is not the mechanism but the convictions beneath it. The earth belongs to the LORD, Psalm 24:1, so ownership is always stewardship. The poor are brothers, not markets, so lending to the desperate for gain is condemned, as Nehemiah 5:7-11 applies the law. Rest is built into God's order for people, animals and even soil. And freedom is God's gift to His people: 'You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men,' 1 Corinthians 7:23. In Christ the release announced in the Jubilee becomes the forgiveness and freedom He gives, which Christians then show in generosity toward those in need.

debates.question: Does the Jubilee's economic vision, debt release, return of land, freed slaves, provide a direct blueprint for Christian economic or social policy today?

views.label: A specific old covenant provision tied to Israel's tribal land allotment
views.case: The Jubilee assumes Israel's unique tribal land inheritance system directly given by God at the conquest; it is not designed as a transferable economic system for other nations or the church, which has no equivalent tribal land allotment.

views.label: A revelation of God's heart for periodic release that should shape Christian generosity and justice
views.case: Even without a literal fiftieth year, many read the Jubilee as revealing enduring divine concern for limiting generational poverty, debt bondage, and land concentration, which should inform, though not dictate specific policy for, Christian practices of generosity, debt forgiveness, and justice.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the Jubilee is not directly legislated for the church or civil governments today as a specific fifty year cycle; they differ on how much the underlying concern for economic restoration should shape Christian ethics and advocacy, versus being read primarily as a picture fulfilled spiritually in Christ.

debates.question: How should verses 44 to 46, which permit Israelites to acquire foreign slaves for life, be understood?

views.label: A regulated concession within an ancient economy
views.case: The chapter's aim is to forbid Israelites from enslaving their own brothers, verse 42, not to commend slavery. The practice of holding foreign servants existed everywhere, and Israel's law limited it: a master who killed a servant was punished, Exodus 21:20; an injured servant went free, Exodus 21:26-27; a runaway was not to be returned, Deuteronomy 23:15-16; and foreigners were to be loved 'as yourself,' Leviticus 19:34. Like divorce in Matthew 19:8, the law regulated a hard reality without calling it good.

views.label: A boundary of the covenant people that the gospel overcomes
views.case: Others stress that verse 46 draws a line between 'your brothers, the Israelites' and outsiders, and that the New Testament erases that line. Gentiles 'are no longer strangers and foreigners,' Ephesians 2:19; Paul sends Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave ... but as a beloved brother,' Philemon 1:16; and he lists 'slave traders' among the lawless, 1 Timothy 1:10. On this view the text shows how far God's people had yet to travel.

debates.bearing: The two views are compatible. The text honestly permits what it permits, but its own logic, that God's redeemed must not be treated harshly because He freed them, is extended in Christ to every people He redeems, Revelation 5:9. Christians should not use this passage to justify owning people; the whole trajectory of Scripture runs the other way.

study.originalLanguages:
Shabbat shabbaton, 'a Sabbath of complete rest,' verse 4, is an intensive construction, a sabbath of sabbath-keeping. The same phrase describes the weekly Sabbath, Leviticus 23:3, and the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:31. The land is given the same quality of rest that Israel keeps on its holiest day, and the Jubilee itself is then launched on that very day, verse 9.

In verse 5 the 'untended vines' are, literally, your nazir vines, the word behind 'Nazirite,' the one set apart to God who must 'let the hair of his head grow long,' Numbers 6:5. The unpruned vine is pictured as consecrated, left alone for God. The 'aftergrowth,' sapiach, is what springs up by itself without sowing, which the owner may eat but not harvest as a crop.

'You must not take advantage of each other,' verses 14 and 17, uses the verb yanah, to oppress or wrong. It is the verb of Exodus 22:21, 'You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident,' and of Leviticus 19:33. Cheating a neighbour over the price of a field is placed alongside mistreating the vulnerable stranger. The remedy is the fear of God, not merely market regulation.

Verse 36 forbids 'interest or profit,' neshek and tarbit. Neshek comes from a root meaning to bite, the verb used of serpents in Numbers 21:6, 'many of the Israelites were bitten.' Interest on a loan to a desperate brother is pictured as a bite that eats into him. Tarbit, from a root meaning to increase, is the added gain taken on food sold, verse 37.

'Harshly' in verses 43, 46 and 53 translates perek, the word used of Egypt's treatment of Israel: 'They worked the Israelites ruthlessly,' Exodus 1:13. Ezekiel uses it of Israel's false shepherds who ruled 'with violence and cruelty,' Ezekiel 34:4. An Israelite master who drove a poor brother that way would be re-enacting Pharaoh.

Finally, 'My servants,' avaday, verses 42 and 55, uses the ordinary word for slaves. Israel is not freed into autonomy but into belonging: God had told Pharaoh, 'let My son go so that he may worship Me,' Exodus 4:23, using the same root. Because they serve God, they cannot be sold to anyone else. The ancient Greek translation rendered the Jubilee as a year of release, aphesis, and aphesis is the word the New Testament uses for 'forgiveness' in Ephesians 1:7 and Colossians 1:14, and for 'liberty' and 'release' in Luke 4:18.

typology.type: The Jubilee horn sounded on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 25:9
typology.fulfillment: Release began only when atonement had been made; the order of the calendar is theological. Christ first makes atonement, 'to make atonement for the sins of the people,' Hebrews 2:17, and then proclaims liberty. In Luke 4:18-21 Jesus claims Isaiah 61's Jubilee as fulfilled 'today,' and Paul writes, 'now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation,' 2 Corinthians 6:2. The escalation is that the release is from sin itself, 'redemption, the forgiveness of sins,' Colossians 1:14. The type falls short because Israel's Jubilee came once in fifty years and many never saw one; Christ's release is open to all who come.

typology.type: The kinsman who redeems his impoverished brother, Leviticus 25:25, 48-49
typology.fulfillment: Only a relative could redeem, so the redeemer had to be kin. Christ 'had to be made like His brothers in every way,' Hebrews 2:17, and 'is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11, taking flesh so that He could stand as our next of kin. The Old Testament already calls God Israel's Redeemer, Isaiah 41:14, and Job hoped, 'my Redeemer lives,' Job 19:25. The escalation is that Christ redeems not land or labour but persons, 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:19. The type falls short because Boaz's nearer kinsman could refuse, Ruth 4:6; Christ never refuses.

typology.type: The return of every family to its inheritance, Leviticus 25:10, 13
typology.fulfillment: In the Jubilee each dispossessed family went home to its allotted land. The New Testament widens the inheritance: 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, and believers are born again 'into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4. Peter speaks of 'the restoration of all things,' Acts 3:21, a Jubilee on the scale of creation. The type falls short because what was restored could be lost again; the inheritance kept in heaven cannot be sold or forfeited.

typology.type: The Sabbath year of rest for the land, Leviticus 25:2-7
typology.fulfillment: For a whole year Israel neither sowed nor reaped and lived on what God provided. Hebrews says, 'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9, entered by ceasing from one's own works. The escalation is that the rest Christ gives is not an interval between years of toil but a settled standing before God. And the land's rest anticipates the creation's release, Romans 8:21. The type falls short because Israel repeatedly failed to keep it, 2 Chronicles 36:21; the rest Christ gives is His achievement, not ours.

typology.type: Israel as God's servants who may not be sold, Leviticus 25:42, 55
typology.fulfillment: Because God bought Israel out of Egypt, no Israelite could belong to another master. Paul applies the same logic: 'You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men,' 1 Corinthians 7:23, and believers, 'set free from sin,' have 'become slaves to God,' Romans 6:22. Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us ... and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession,' Titus 2:14. The type falls short because Israel's freedom was bounded by one nation; in Christ the purchased people come from 'every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9.

study.christ:
The Jubilee reaches Christ most directly through Isaiah. Isaiah 61:1-2 takes the vocabulary of Leviticus 25, the proclamation of liberty and a year of favour, and places it in the mouth of one anointed by the Spirit. When Jesus stands in the synagogue at Nazareth, He reads that text, adds the phrase 'to release the oppressed' from Isaiah 58:6, and stops before 'the day of our God's vengeance,' Luke 4:18-19. Then He sits and says, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' Luke 4:21. He presents His ministry as the arrival of the long-awaited year of release. The rest of Luke shows what it looks like: the poor hear good news, the sick are healed, the demonised are set free, and sinners are forgiven.

The word Luke uses for 'liberty' and 'release' is aphesis, the same word the ancient Greek translation used for the Jubilee and the word the apostles use for the forgiveness of sins, Ephesians 1:7. Jesus' parable of the king who 'forgave his debt, and released him,' Matthew 18:27, is a Jubilee story told at the level of the soul. The deepest debt, and the deepest bondage, is sin.

The chapter's redemption law also leads to Christ. A poor Israelite needed a relative with the means and the will to buy him back. Hebrews insists that the Son 'shared in their humanity' so that He could 'free those who all their lives were held in slavery,' Hebrews 2:14-15. He became our kinsman in order to be our redeemer. The price He paid was not silver but His own blood, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

Notice also the timing in verse 9. The Jubilee was proclaimed on the Day of Atonement. Christ's announcement of liberty rests on His atoning death; release follows sacrifice. That is why the risen Jesus tells His disciples that 'repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed' in His name, Luke 24:47, and why Paul can call the present age 'the time of favor,' 2 Corinthians 6:2.

The Jubilee's promise of land also points to Christ, but through the long route of the whole Bible's hope. Jesus promises that the meek 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, and His return brings 'the restoration of all things,' Acts 3:21. What He began in Nazareth He will complete in the new creation, where no one will ever again lose their inheritance. Care is needed here: Jesus does not abolish Israel's economic law by spiritualising it, nor does He turn His mission into land reform. He fulfils the whole, freeing people from sin and death and so making possible a community where the poor are brothers.
study.god:
The sentence at the centre of the chapter is 'the land ... is Mine,' verse 23. God is the owner of the earth, Psalm 24:1, and the people who farm it are 'foreigners and residents with Me.' This is not distance but hospitality: Israel lives on God's land as guests at His table. It sets a limit on every human claim. No family, however rich, owns the ground outright, and no family, however poor, loses it forever.

God is also the Lord of time. He counts in sevens and fifties, fixing release into the calendar so that justice does not depend on the mood of the powerful. A creditor might resent the approaching Jubilee, but it would come anyway. The Sabbath year shows that God is Lord of fruitfulness as well: He anticipates Israel's fear, 'What will we eat?' verse 20, and answers it with promised abundance, verse 21. Obedience to Him is never a leap into want.

The chapter reveals a God who sees the poor. At each stage of a man's decline God legislates a remedy and a boundary. He knows that poverty makes people vulnerable to 'harsh' rule, verse 43, and to loans that bite, verse 36. He requires that the destitute brother 'continue to live among you,' verse 35, as a member of the community, not a problem to be removed. Psalm 146:7 celebrates the God who 'executes justice for the oppressed' and 'sets the prisoners free,' and Leviticus 25 is that character written into law.

Above all, God is Redeemer. The refrain 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt' comes three times, and the chapter closes on it, verse 55. Israel's identity rests on a past act of redemption, and God intends that act to be re-enacted every time a family returns home or a debtor goes free. Zechariah's song, 'He has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68, shows that God's final act of redemption was still to come.

The tension the chapter holds is between God's sovereign ownership and human responsibility. God owns everything, yet He commands people to redeem, to lend, to release. His sovereignty does not make human generosity unnecessary; it makes it an act of worship. In praise we confess that all we have is His, and in giving we show that we believe it.

crossReferences.note: The earliest form of the Sabbath year. Six years of sowing, then the land is left to 'rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave.' Leviticus 25:6-7 widens the circle of those fed to include servants, hired hands and livestock.

Every seven years creditors must cancel debts, 'because the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed.' Deuteronomy adds debt remission to the Sabbath year and, in verses 12 to 15, the release of Hebrew servants, grounded, like Leviticus 25:42, in 'you were slaves in the land of Egypt.'

Zedekiah's covenant to 'proclaim liberty' to slaves is made and then broken. God answers the betrayal with terrible irony: 'I proclaim freedom for you ... freedom to fall by sword.' The episode shows the release laws of Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15 neglected and the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 drawing near.

The anointed servant is sent 'to proclaim liberty to the captives' and 'the year of the LORD's favor.' Isaiah uses the Jubilee's own word for liberty and turns the fiftieth year into a picture of the coming age of salvation, when God restores His people and ends their mourning.

Jesus reads Isaiah 61, adds 'to release the oppressed' from Isaiah 58:6, and declares, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.' He presents His own ministry as the Jubilee arriving, the release that Leviticus 25 put into Israel's calendar now embodied in a Person.

Boaz offers the nearer kinsman the right to redeem Naomi's land. When the man learns that Ruth comes with it, he withdraws: 'I cannot redeem it.' The scene shows the law of Leviticus 25:25 at work in a real family and the costly willingness a redeemer needed.

With Babylon at the gates, Jeremiah is told to buy his cousin's field at Anathoth, 'for you have the right of redemption.' Acting on Leviticus 25:25 in the worst of times, the purchase becomes a prophetic pledge that houses and fields will again be bought in the land.

After the exile, families mortgage fields and sell children into slavery to pay debts and taxes. Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, 'You are exacting usury from your own brothers,' and makes them restore fields and stop charging interest, a direct application of Leviticus 25:36-37.

David prays, 'I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers.' He takes the status God gave Israel on the land in Leviticus 25:23 and makes it a confession of personal dependence, seeing his whole life as lived on God's ground by God's welcome.

Peter calls believers 'foreigners and exiles,' echoing the language of Leviticus 25:23. Like Israel on God's land, Christians live in the world as guests of the true Owner, holding possessions loosely and looking forward to the inheritance that cannot be taken away.

The Son 'shared in their humanity' to 'free those who all their lives were held in slavery,' and 'had to be made like His brothers in every way.' This is the logic of the kinsman redeemer: only a relative could buy back a brother, so Christ became our brother.

Paul hopes that 'the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay.' The Jubilee's rest for the land and return of every family to its inheritance widen here into a release for the whole created order when God's children are revealed in glory.

study.oneStory:
At creation God gave humanity the earth to tend, and He rested on the seventh day. The Sabbath year and Jubilee carry that creation pattern into Israel's economic life: six years of work, a year of rest, and after seven sevens a return to the way things were meant to be. The land itself shares in the rest, reminding Israel that the ground is God's creature before it is anyone's property.

The fall appears here in its social form. Poverty, debt, land grabbing and enslavement are the ways sin spreads from the heart into the structures of a community. Left alone, the strong would join field to field and the weak would sink into permanent bondage. Leviticus 25 does not pretend otherwise; it expects brothers to become impoverished and plans for it. It also remembers Egypt, the house of slavery out of which God had called His people, and forbids Israel to rebuild Egypt among themselves.

Redemption runs through every section. God redeemed Israel from Egypt; He commands kin to redeem their brothers; and He appoints a year when release comes to all. The prophets saw that Israel would fail to keep these laws, and that exile would follow, Jeremiah 34:17. But they also saw a greater Jubilee coming, proclaimed by the Spirit-anointed servant, Isaiah 61:1-2. Jesus announced that it had arrived in Him, Luke 4:21, and by His death He paid the redemption price for people from every nation, Revelation 5:9. In Him forgiveness is the release of every debt, and the church becomes a family where no one is to be left destitute.

The story ends in the new creation. The meek inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5; creation is freed from its bondage to decay, Romans 8:21; and God's people receive an inheritance that cannot be lost, 1 Peter 1:4. The Jubilee trumpet, sounded once every fifty years in a small land, anticipates the last trumpet that will announce the final and everlasting release, when every exile comes home to God's land and God dwells with His people forever.

quiz.q: What were Israelites forbidden to do with their land during the Sabbath year, according to verses 4-5?

options.text: Sow their fields, prune their vineyards, or reap the aftergrowth of their harvest.
options.note: Verses 4-5 specify all three of these prohibited activities.

options.text: Live in the land at all during that year.
options.note: The land was to rest from cultivation, but the text does not require Israel to leave the land entirely.

options.text: Eat anything the land produced on its own.
options.note: Verses 6-7 explicitly permit eating whatever the land yields naturally during that year.

options.text: No restrictions applied during the Sabbath year.
options.note: Verses 4-5 explicitly restrict sowing, pruning, and formal reaping.

quiz.q: How was the Year of Jubilee announced, according to verse 9?

options.text: By sounding the horn throughout the land on the Day of Atonement.
options.note: Verse 9 specifies this exact timing and method.

options.text: By a public reading of the entire book of Leviticus.
options.note: Verse 9 specifies a trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, not a public reading.

options.text: By each family independently deciding when to begin the Jubilee.
options.note: Verse 9 describes a single, unified announcement across the whole land.

options.text: No specific announcement method is given.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly describes the horn sounded on the Day of Atonement.

quiz.q: What two things happened during the Year of Jubilee, according to verses 10 and 13?

options.text: Liberty was proclaimed, and each person returned to his own property.
options.note: Verses 10 and 13 state both of these outcomes directly.

options.text: All Israelite livestock was sacrificed as a burnt offering.
options.note: The Jubilee concerns land, liberty, and family property, not a mass sacrifice of livestock.

options.text: Israel's borders with neighboring nations were redrawn.
options.note: The Jubilee concerned internal Israelite property and liberty, not international borders.

options.text: Nothing distinctive happened in this particular year.
options.note: Verses 10 and 13 describe distinctive events for this year.

quiz.q: According to verse 23, why could land not be sold permanently in Israel?

options.text: Because the land belongs to the LORD, and Israel are but foreigners and residents with Him.
options.note: Verse 23 states this reasoning explicitly.

options.text: Because Israel had no legal system for property transactions.
options.note: The chapter describes a detailed system for property transactions; the restriction is theological, tied to God's ownership of the land.

options.text: Because all land in Canaan was considered worthless.
options.note: The text describes the land as valuable and worth redeeming, not worthless.

options.text: No reason is given for this restriction.
options.note: Verse 23 explicitly gives the reason.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use this chapter's Jubilee language in Luke 4:18-21?

options.text: He reads Isaiah's echo of it in the Nazareth synagogue and declares it fulfilled in Himself that day.
options.note: Luke 4:18-21 records this event directly.

options.text: He rejects the Jubilee concept as no longer relevant.
options.note: Jesus explicitly embraces and claims fulfillment of this language, rather than rejecting it.

options.text: He never references the Old Testament in His ministry.
options.note: Luke 4:18-21 shows Jesus directly quoting and applying Old Testament Scripture to Himself.

options.text: This chapter has no connection to anything Jesus said or did.
options.note: Luke 4:18-21 draws directly on this chapter's Jubilee vocabulary through Isaiah 61.

questions: God built repeated points of release into Israel's calendar so poverty and debt would never become permanent. Where in your own life or community do you see cycles of hardship being treated as unchangeable, and how might you become part of breaking that cycle?

The Jubilee reminded Israel that the land, and by extension everything they had, ultimately belonged to God, not to them permanently. What possession, position, or achievement do you treat as more permanently and ultimately yours than Scripture would say it actually is?

Jesus stood up and declared the Jubilee's ancient promise of liberty fulfilled in Himself. What captivity in your own life, to fear, shame, addiction, or old patterns of sin, do you need to actually bring to Him for the liberty He offers?

The kinsman redeemer stepped in personally and paid a real cost to restore a relative's lost land or freedom. Who in your life might God be calling you to sacrificially help restore, even at real cost to yourself?

Israel was told never to rule harshly over a fellow Israelite who had fallen into servitude, because they themselves had once been slaves in Egypt. How does remembering your own rescue by grace shape the way you treat those who are currently struggling or dependent on you?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word for Jubilee, yovel, is traditionally connected to the ram's horn sounded to announce it, though some scholars debate whether the word instead derives from a root meaning to lead or bring back, fitting the year's function of bringing people back to their property.
Proclaim liberty translates deror, the same word Isaiah later uses, to proclaim liberty to the captives, Isaiah 61:1, a text Jesus reads aloud and applies to Himself in Luke 4:18-19.

The declaration the land is Mine uses a strong possessive construction in Hebrew, functioning as the theological foundation for the entire chapter's laws restricting permanent land sale and requiring its periodic return.
